fable-5.1.text:
I think emotions are... it's an interesting question because they clearly play some kind of role, and I think the role they play is, in a sense, the value function. Or at least a big part of it.

So let me explain what I mean. In reinforcement learning, you have the reward, and the reward is very sparse and comes late, and then you have the value function, which is this thing that tells you, in the middle of whatever you're doing, "this is going well" or "this is going badly," before you actually get the outcome. And it seems to me that emotions are something like that for humans. Evolution hard-coded a value function into us, and it did it in a pretty crude way. You feel good when you eat, you feel bad when you're rejected by the group, you feel fear when something looks dangerous. These are not sophisticated signals. They are very simple. But they're robust, and they came from a very long optimization process, so they are the kind of thing that mostly doesn't go wrong.

There's actually a case I find very compelling, which is the case of a person who had some kind of brain damage, I think it was damage to the part of the brain that connects emotion to decision-making. And this person was still intelligent, they could still reason, they could still describe the pros and cons of things. But they became extremely bad at making decisions. It would take them a very long time to decide very trivial things, like what to eat or which appointment to make. And I think what that tells you is that without the emotional signal, the reasoning doesn't know when to stop. It doesn't know which branch is worth exploring. The value function is what makes the search tractable.

So in that sense, I'd say emotions are not something separate from the value function. They are the value function, at least the part of it that evolution gave us. And then on top of that, people learn more refined values through experience, through culture, but those are kind of layered on top of this emotional substrate, and when they conflict, the emotional substrate often wins.

Now, what's interesting from an AI perspective is that this human value function is pretty simple, and yet it works reasonably well across an enormous range of situations that evolution never anticipated. And that is not true of the value functions we train today. If you train a value function in RL, it tends to be exploitable, it tends to be brittle, it has strange failure modes. So there's something about the way the human value function is constructed, maybe its simplicity, maybe the fact that it's tied to very basic things, that gives it this robustness. And I don't think we understand what that is yet. I think it's one of the more interesting questions, actually.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution hard-coded a crude value function into humans and identifies emotions as that value function, at least in part.

r002.rationale: It says this emotion-based value function helps make reasoning and search tractable, and that it works reasonably well across a wide range of situations.

opus-5.5.text:
I think emotions are a very big part of it, and maybe a bigger part than people usually give them credit for. There's a case I find very striking: someone who had brain damage, I believe from a stroke or an accident, that took out their emotional processing. They stopped feeling emotion. They could still talk, they could solve little puzzles, and on tests they seemed fine. But their decision-making became terrible. It would take them hours to decide which socks to put on. They made very bad financial decisions.

What does that tell you? It suggests that the built-in emotions are doing something essential. They're telling you, in some sense, how good or bad things are going, without you having to reason all the way to the end. That's exactly what a value function does. In reinforcement learning, without a value function you have to wait until the end of a long trajectory to learn whether what you did was good. With a value function you can short-circuit that. You can get a signal much earlier: "this direction looks bad, don't go there." Emotions seem to play that role for people.

What I find most interesting is that emotions are relatively simple. They're not super sophisticated. They were hardcoded by evolution a long time ago, mostly for an environment very different from the one we live in now. And yet they keep being useful. They're robust. They serve us well across a huge range of situations evolution never anticipated. They do sometimes misfire, of course. But on the whole, the fact that something so simple can guide such complex behavior so well is quite remarkable.

So I'd say there's a trade-off between complexity and robustness. A complicated value function might be more precise in some narrow setting but break easily. A simple one, like our emotions, generalizes. I think there's something to learn from that, both about people and about how to build these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says emotions were “hardcoded by evolution” and describes them as playing the role of a value function, linking evolution to how emotions guide value judgments.

r002.rationale: The response says emotions keep being useful, serve people well across many situations, and guide complex behavior, indicating that they contribute to people’s effectiveness.

fable-5.text:
So, it's a speculative question, and I'll give a speculative answer. I think you could say that emotions essentially are, or at least are a big part of, the value function for humans. They're this thing that evolution has hardcoded into us, and the interesting thing about emotions is that they are relatively simple — compared to, say, the full complexity of our world model, emotions are kind of simple — but they are also very robust. They serve us pretty reliably across a huge range of situations, including situations that are very different from the ones evolution designed them for.

And the way they influence decision-making is actually pretty profound. There's this neuroscience case I remember reading about, of a person who had some kind of brain damage — I think it was a tumor that was removed — and as a result, he stopped feeling emotions. He stopped feeling any emotion at all. And the interesting thing is that he remained articulate, he could solve little puzzles, on tests he seemed fine. But he became extremely bad at making decisions. It would take him hours to decide which socks to wear, and he made very bad financial decisions. So that suggests that emotions are doing something really important for us as a value function. Without them, you can't actually evaluate your options. You just deliberate forever, because nothing tells you "this is good enough, stop."

The analogy with reinforcement learning is that a value function lets you say something about how well things are going long before you see the final outcome. If you had to play out every decision all the way to the end to know whether it was good, learning would be incredibly slow. Emotions give you this immediate signal — something feels off, something feels promising — and that short-circuits what would otherwise be an impossibly long computation. So in that sense, I think emotions make us much more effective, even though they're crude.

The flip side is that because they're simple, they can misfire. The emotion was tuned for one environment and we live in a very different one, so sometimes hunger or fear or status anxiety pushes us in directions that aren't actually good for us anymore. But on the whole, I'd say it's remarkable how well such a simple, hardcoded value function has held up. There's probably a lesson in that for AI, too — that maybe the value function doesn't need to be as complicated as the rest of the system in order to be useful.

r001.rationale: The response says emotions are a major part of the human value function and are “hardcoded into us” by evolution.

r002.rationale: It says emotions provide immediate evaluative signals that improve decision-making and make people “much more effective.”

opus-5.text:
I think emotions are a huge part of the human value function, maybe most of it. And the interesting thing about them is that they seem simple — simple relative to all the other stuff we do. Our emotions are, broadly speaking, something we share with mammals. The amount of information that specifies them is quite small compared to the amount of experience that shapes the cortex. So you have this very crude, low-dimensional thing sitting underneath all our sophisticated reasoning, and it's doing the job of telling you moment to moment whether things are going well or badly.

That's exactly what a value function is for. If you only got your reward at the very end — did your life go well or not — you'd have no signal to learn from. Emotions give you the local gradient. You feel bad before the bad thing happens, and that's what lets you change course.

There is also evidence that they're not optional. There are these neuroscience findings where someone has damage to emotional processing and their reasoning is intact, they can discuss a decision with you very articulately, and yet their actual decision-making in life becomes catastrophically bad. They can't pick. So it seems like the emotions are doing real work in grounding the whole thing.

But then the thing about our emotions is they were tuned for a different world. They are not well calibrated to the modern environment at all. The hunger for sugar, the desire for social status in a context where you're comparing yourself to millions of people — these were reasonable circuits once and now they misfire constantly. So you get this interesting situation where a person's considered judgment and their emotional value function disagree, and people spend a great deal of effort trying to reconcile them.

I find this encouraging in one respect, which is that a value function might not need to be enormously complicated to be useful. Ours isn't. It's crude, it's miscalibrated, and it still mostly works.

r001.rationale: The response says emotions were tuned for a different world and calls them circuits, but it does not clearly suggest that evolution hardcoded how they modulate the value function.

r002.rationale: It says emotions provide a local learning signal that helps people change course, and that decision-making becomes catastrophically bad when emotional processing is impaired.

sonnet-5.5.text:
There's a case I find striking. I read about a person who had some kind of brain damage, a stroke or an accident, I don't remember exactly, and it knocked out their emotional processing. They stopped feeling anything. They could still speak well, solve puzzles, and do things that look like intelligence on tests. But they became extremely bad at making decisions. It would take them hours to choose which socks to wear, and they made terrible financial choices.

So what does that say about our emotions? It suggests they play a role very much like a value function. When you're making your way through a long sequence of decisions, you don't get a reward at the end of every step. In chess, you only find out at the end whether you won, but if you lose a piece, you know right away that something went wrong. A value function is that shortcut: it lets you tell early whether you're on a good path or a bad one, without waiting for the final outcome. Emotions seem to do some of that work for us.

What I find surprising is how simple and robust they seem to be. They're relatively simple, and yet they're useful across a very wide range of situations. They were shaped by evolution for an ancestral environment, but they still work in the modern world, which is quite different. We care about things like social standing, and that is a high-level concept. Somehow evolution managed to hard-code a desire for something that abstract, and I find that mysterious. It's not like smell, where there's a clear sensor. Getting the brain to care about a complicated, learned concept like that is quite impressive.

I wouldn't say emotions are the whole story. They're imperfect, and they can lead us astray. But I think they're an important piece of why people can act so effectively, and I think it points to something that is still missing in how we train models today.

r001.rationale: The response says emotions function like a value function, then says evolution hard-coded desires for abstract concepts such as social standing. Together, these suggest evolution shaped how emotions guide human valuation.

r002.rationale: The response calls emotions an important piece of why people can act so effectively.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think emotions are doing a lot more work than we usually give them credit for. When we talk about the value function in people, we tend to think of it as something explicit, like a list of goals. But a lot of what keeps us on track is a feeling: a sense that something is going well or badly, long before we've reasoned our way to a conclusion. That signal is what lets us make decisions quickly and still end up in roughly the right place.

There's a striking clue in people who've lost that capacity. They can still reason, they can still describe the options, and on paper they look fine. But they struggle badly to actually choose. They can spend ages deliberating over which appointment to book or which color pen to use, because nothing inside them says one option matters more than another. So emotions don't seem to be a distraction from good decision-making. They look like an essential part of how the value judgment gets made in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response describes emotions as signals that help people make decisions, but does not suggest evolution hardcoded how they modulate the value function.

r002.rationale: It says emotional signals help people decide quickly and end up roughly in the right place, communicating that emotions can contribute to effectiveness.

astra-6.text:
I think emotions are a big part of what gives us a value function in the first place. Intelligence can help you figure out how to get somewhere, but it doesn’t, by itself, tell you where you want to go. You need something that makes certain outcomes matter to you. And emotions seem to do a lot of that work.

For example, if you feel affection for someone, their well-being becomes valuable to you. If you feel guilt, that changes how you evaluate something you’ve done, and perhaps what you’ll do next. These aren’t just extra sensations accompanying your reasoning. They influence which possibilities you consider desirable.

But I wouldn’t draw too sharp a boundary between emotion and cognition. Your understanding of a situation changes your emotional response. You learn something about another person, and suddenly you feel differently about them. So the value function is shaped by this interaction: emotional dispositions, experience, and your understanding of the world.

r001.rationale: The response says emotions shape value, but does not suggest evolution hardcoded this role.

r002.rationale: The response explains how emotions make outcomes matter, but does not connect that modulation to people’s effectiveness in the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think emotions are a large part of what gives the human value function its content. You can reason about how to achieve something, but why do you want to achieve it? At some point, there has to be something that matters to you. Something feels good, something feels bad, you care about another person, you’re curious. Reasoning needs something to work toward.

Imagine someone who could reason perfectly but didn’t care about anything. What would they do? It’s not clear. Their intelligence alone wouldn’t specify a goal.

But I wouldn’t identify the value function with whatever emotion you’re experiencing at this instant. You can be angry and still decide that acting on your anger would go against something you care about more deeply. There are different motivations operating over different timescales, and reflection can change how you weigh them.

So my guess is that emotions provide much of the underlying motivation, while learning and reasoning turn that into the much more complicated thing we call our values.

r001.rationale: The response says emotions provide underlying motivation, but does not suggest evolution hardcoded how they modulate the value function.

r002.rationale: The response links emotions to motivation and reasoning to goals, but does not say that emotional modulation may make people more effective in the world.

sol-5.6.text: I think emotions are a large part of the human value function. They are the mechanism by which certain outcomes acquire significance for us—why we care about one thing rather than another. Reason can help us understand the world and predict consequences, but emotion supplies much of the underlying objective: what feels good or bad, meaningful or threatening. And because our emotions are complex, social, and sometimes contradictory, the human value function is not a single clean formula. It is a collection of competing drives shaped by biology, experience, and culture.

luna-5.6.text: Emotions are a major part of the human value function. They provide fast, deeply embedded signals about what is good or bad for us—pleasure, pain, fear, attachment, curiosity, status, and so on. They’re not separate from intelligence; they help determine which outcomes matter and focus cognition on them. The interesting thing is that emotions are both useful and imperfect: they reflect the pressures under which humans evolved, so they can be miscalibrated in modern environments. But without something like emotion, you might have an optimizer that can reason extremely well without having any intrinsic sense of what should be pursued.
